activities.anchor: Strip away the variety and one process remains
activities.caption: drag between the surplus and the deficit
activities.name: aeTransitCompare

config.prompt: One conveyor, two ends — drag between them:

before.label: the tropics — surplus
before.text: Far more solar energy per square metre than the poles receive. The atmosphere, helped by the ocean, is the conveyor that evens the difference out.

after.label: the poles — deficit
after.text: The other end of the same conveyor: every wind that has ever blown is part of the evening-out, and a hurricane is that conveyor running in overdrive.

config.why: Weather is the atmosphere moving energy from where there is too much to where there is too little — the drama is weather; the bookkeeping is meteorology.

activities.anchor: on a classroom globe, the thickness of the varnish
activities.caption: call the mass squeezed into the bottom floor
activities.name: aeMassEstimate

config.prompt: The atmosphere's total mass is about 5.1 × 10¹⁸ kg, and 99% lies below 30 km. Roughly what share of that mass is crammed into the lowest 5–6 km?
config.why: Half — the film is squeezed densest at the bottom, which is why pressure halves roughly every 5.5 km and Everest's summit at 8.85 km carries only about a third of sea-level pressure.
config.context: Yet that film moves more energy per day than humanity consumes in years.

activities.caption: file each constituent by its atmospheric role
activities.name: aeCompositionBuckets

config.prompt: A thin, dry-ish, mostly-two-gas skin — file each constituent:
buckets: bulk: N₂ and O₂ — radiatively invisible

items.label: nitrogen, 78% — neither absorbs nor emits significant infrared
CO₂, about 420 parts per million and climbing
clouds of droplets and ice; aerosols — dust, smoke, salt, sulfate
0–4% depending on place and day — the only component that changes phase at Earth temperatures

config.why: The inversion worth internalising: the trace constituents matter more than the bulk — the single most useful fact for understanding both weather and climate.

activities.anchor: not by altitude marks on a diagram
activities.caption: pair each layer with what heats it
activities.name: aeLayersMatch

config.prompt: Each layer's personality follows from its heater — pair them:

pairs.right: heated from below — turbulent, well-mixed, holding virtually all the weather
heated from within — ozone absorbs ultraviolet, so temperature rises with height
cools to the coldest temperatures on Earth, below −90 °C — meteors burn up here
heated directly by extreme ultraviolet and X-rays — the aurora and the ISS live here

config.why: The boundaries are found with a thermometer, not a ruler: a layer's top is where the temperature turns — and the tropopause runs from about 8 km over the poles to about 18 km over the tropics.

activities.anchor: which we do not feel because it presses from every direction
activities.caption: set the halfway mark of the column on the altitude scale
activities.name: aeHalfPlace

config.prompt: Pressure is the weight of the air above. At roughly what altitude does half the atmosphere's mass still lie above you — and half below?
config.why: About 5.5 km — the 500 hPa surface, a coordinate meteorologists use as naturally as altitude. From there the pressure halves roughly every 5.5 km, because compressible air packs denser at the bottom.

activities.caption: one line of the map-reading note overstates the highs
activities.name: aeIsobarSpot

config.prompt: A map-reading note — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: A strong high (1040 hPa) beside a deep low (960 hPa) differs by only about 8% from the mean.
Yet those differences, mapped as isobars, drive every wind from sea breeze to hurricane.
The 500 hPa surface sits about 5.5 km up, where half the mass lies below.
Because the highs and lows are so different in size, a deep low reaches only about half the pressure of a strong high.
A pressure level is a physical surface that maps, balloons and models can all follow.
config.correction: Horizontal pressure differences are small — about 8% from the mean at the extremes — yet mighty: they drive every wind. (The halving-with-height of the vertical column is a different measurement from the horizontal map.)
config.why: Small percentages, large consequences — the weather map's actual information content lives in those isobars.

activities.caption: call the sea-surface temperature that switches the machine on
activities.name: aeFuelEstimate

config.prompt: A hurricane is a machine for releasing latent heat. Above roughly what sea-surface temperature (°C) does that machine find its fuel?
config.why: About 26–27 °C. The channel is enormous: evaporating water absorbs some 2.26 million joules per kilogram — energy that travels invisibly as vapour and is released all at once wherever the vapour condenses.
config.context: Condensation, not sunlight, is the direct fuel of storms.

config.text: A rising parcel cools not by mixing with its surroundings but by %%0%%: it moves into lower pressure, expands, and the work of pushing comes from its own internal energy. Descending air warms by the same physics — compression rather than contact — which is why air flowing down a mountain range arrives %%1%% and %%2%% (the foehn and chinook winds).
config.hint: The first blank names the mechanism; the last two describe the wind.
